property_summary: For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true when interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (specifically it returns true for IERC165 and for IAccessControl), while the mutant always returns false and thus violates this for those interfaceIds.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference C returns true when asked about IERC165's interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId) or IAccessControl's interface id (type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) according to inherited logic, whereas the mutant that always returns false will return false for at least those ids; the test fuzzes an interfaceId and asserts that if it equals IERC165's or IAccessControl's interface id then supportsInterface returns true (which the mutant breaks).
For every interfaceId, if it equals IERC165's interfaceId then C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true (reference) whereas the mutant that always returns false will return false for that input.
For any bytes4 interfaceId, if it equals type(IERC165).interfaceId then C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true; the mutant that always returns false will violate this for that interfaceId.

For any bytes4 interfaceId, the correct C reports true when queried for IERC165's interface id or IAccessControl's interface id (i.e., supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) and supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) are true); the mutant that always returns false will return false for those ids, so there exist inputs (those exact interface ids) where the mutant breaks this rule.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract's supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true iff the interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e., it does NOT always return true); the mutant that always returns true violates this by returning true for interfaceIds that the reference would return false for.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true from supportsInterface exactly when the id equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (or is supported by super), whereas the mutant returns true for all interfaceIds — so there exist interfaceIds for which reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract's supportsInterface either returns true only for actually supported interfaces (i.e., IERC165, IAccessControl, or those supported by super) while the mutant that always returns true will report true for some interfaceId values that the reference reports false for; thus there exists some interfaceId where reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract's supportsInterface either returns true or false according to actual supported interfaces (it does not always return true), whereas the mutant returns true for all interfaceIds, so there exist interfaceIds for which the reference returns false but the mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the correct contract's supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns false for at least some interfaceIds that it does not implement, whereas the mutant returns true for all interfaceIds — therefore there exist interfaceIds where reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true for IERC165's interfaceId exactly when interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId implies supportsInterface returns true (i.e., supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) == true) while the mutant flips this result and will return false for that id; therefore the reference always reports support for IERC165 but the mutant does not for that specific input.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true when queried with IERC165's interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId) or any id that super.supportsInterface recognizes, while the mutant negates the check and will return false for IERC165's id; the test fuzzes an arbitrary bytes4 and asserts that calling supportsInterface with that value on the deployed contract does not revert and that for the specific IERC165 id the reference returns true (a value the mutant will flip).

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference contract's supportsInterface does not revert and, specifically, it always returns true when queried with type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant flips the IERC165 check and will return false for that particular id, so a fuzzed bytes4 that equals type(IERC165).interfaceId distinguishes them.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) never reverts; in particular the reference contract always returns true for interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId, while the mutant returns false for that specific id, so supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) == true is a universal property of the reference that the mutant violates for that input.

For any queried bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface never reverts and in particular returns true when queried with the IERC165 interface id; the mutant flips the IERC165 check and will return false for that specific id, so the property is violated for interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId.

For any role and account, the reference contract always reports hasRole(role, account) based on that role's members mapping (i.e., whether the account itself has the role); the mutant instead reports membership of the role's adminRole, so there exist role/account pairs where the reference returns true but the mutant returns false (or vice versa).

For any role and account, the reference contract's hasRole returns whether the account is a member (true iff member); the mutant inverts this result so for some inputs the returned boolean is different (i.e., reference.hasRole(role, acct) == !mutant.hasRole(role, acct)).

For any role and account, the correct contract returns hasRole(role, account)==true exactly when that account is recorded as a member; the mutant inverts the boolean so for some (role,account) the returned value differs (true vs false).

For any role/account, hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract equals the stored membership boolean (true iff member); the mutant inverts that boolean, so there exist role/account pairs for which the returned value differs (specifically for accounts that actually have the role).

For any role and account, hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract returns true for accounts which are recorded as members and false otherwise; the mutant negates that boolean so there exist role/account pairs (e.g. an account that actually has a role) for which the returned value is inverted and thus different.

For every role/account pair, a correct Timelock C returns hasRole(role, account) == true exactly when that account is recorded as a role member; the mutant inverts the returned boolean, so there exist fuzzed (role,account) pairs for which the returned value is negated and thus differs (e.g., an account that actually has the role will return false).

For every (role, account) the reference contract returns whether that account currently has the role (i.e. returns false for most arbitrary pairs unless previously granted), but the mutant always returns true for every pair, so there exist inputs where hasRole(role, account) is false in the reference yet true in the mutant.

For every role/account pair, the correct contract's hasRole either returns true only when that role was set up for that account (not universally true); specifically, there exist role/account inputs for which hasRole returns false on the reference but the mutant (which always returns true) would differ — we assert that for any fuzzed role and account, calling hasRole with those params does not always succeed in returning true unless the account is one of the preconfigured roles (we check that at least one fuzzed pair yields false on the reference, which the mutant would break).

For every (role, account) pair the deployed Timelock returns a boolean from hasRole; the reference C can return false for some pairs (not everyone has every role), while the mutant always returns true — so there exist fuzzed (role, account) inputs where reference.hasRole(role,account) == false but mutant.hasRole(...) == true.

For any arbitrary role and account, the reference contract's hasRole either returns true only for accounts that were explicitly granted that role (including DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to deployer and contract) and false otherwise; specifically, there exists at least one role/account pair for which reference.hasRole(role, account) == false (so not everyone has every role), whereas the mutant always returns true and thus will disagree on such pairs — the test fuzzes role and account and asserts that hasRole(role, account) is false (a property always true for some inputs on the reference but violated by the mutant).

For any arbitrary role (bytes32) and account (address) the reference contract may legitimately report that the account does NOT have that role for many inputs; specifically, there exists at least one (role, account) pair for which C.hasRole(role, account) returns false — the mutant that always returns true will violate that by returning true for such inputs.

For any (role, account) the reference contract's hasRole returns whether that account currently holds the role (i.e., can be true for some inputs); the mutant always returns false so there exist inputs (role, account) where reference.hasRole(...) == true but mutant.hasRole(...) == false.

For any role and account where the contract has previously granted that role to the account, hasRole(role, account) returns true in the reference contract; the mutant always returns false, so it will report false for some (role, account) that the reference reports true.

For any role and account, once the contract has been set up to grant a specific role to that account, calling hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract always returns true; the mutant that always returns false will report false for some (role, account) that the reference reports true.

For any role and account, if the contract itself (address(c)) was granted that role during construction, hasRole(role, account) returns true for that account on the reference but the mutant (which always returns false) will report false for some fuzzed (role,account) pair — so the property: 'address(c) (the contract) has DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE' is always true in reference and broken by the mutant.

For any bytes32 role the contract sets up in constructor, calling hasRole(role, address(this)) always returns true on the correct contract (the contract was granted TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE in setup), whereas the mutant that always returns false will report false for that same (role, address(c)) for some fuzzed role value equal to the TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE constant — so the general rule is: hasRole(TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE, address(c)) == true for the deployed contract, which the mutant breaks.

For any role and any account, the reference contract returns whether that exact account has the role (hasRole(role, account) == _roles[role].members[account]); the mutant instead always returns whether the zero address has the role, so there exist inputs (accounts not equal to address(0)) for which hasRole(role, account) differs from the reference.

For any role and any account, the correct contract's hasRole(role, account) returns whether that exact account holds the role; the mutant instead always returns the membership of address(0), so there exist accounts for which the two results differ.

For every (role, account) pair the reference contract returns whether that exact account has the role (hasRole(role, account) == membership of that account), whereas the mutant always returns the membership of address(0) so there exist fuzzed accounts for which hasRole(role, account) differs.

For any role and any account, the correct contract returns whether that specific account has the role (hasRole(role, account) reads membership[account]); the mutant incorrectly always reads membership[address(0)], so there exist fuzzed account inputs where hasRole(role, account) differs and the test will catch that.
